speaker: andrewday
text: Thank you, Mayor. Given the review of the governance rules tonight, the council meeting prayer has not been removed, despite the fact the new Local Government Act 2020 does not provide the authority of a council to do this. Division 1-A3 of the Local Government Act 2020 stipulates in performing its role, a council may A, perform any duties or functions or exercise any powers conferred on a council by or under this act or any other act. And B, perform any other functions that the council determines are necessary to enable the council to perform its role. There are no sections within this act or any other act that provides the power to make any religious statement or choose what religion of the council by having a prayer of one religion. Therefore, it can be seen to be illegal to do so, unless of course it is deemed by the council necessary to enable the council to perform its role. There's two questions to this. Question number one, does the council believe it's necessary for council to perform its role to hold a prayer at the beginning of the meeting and therefore claiming it's legally through this clause in the act? Question two, does the council believe it is not discriminatory to have a Christian prayer at the beginning of the meeting and therefore imposing one particular religious statement on everyone present when viewers, council staff and other councillors may not be believers or are of other faiths than Christian and therefore pushing one religion's agenda?

speaker: andrewconlon
text: Thank you for your question. And I will ask Mr. Andrew McMaster, Group Manager for Governance and Risk to respond.

speaker: andrewmcmaster
text: Thank you, Mayor. And thank you for your question. The Local Government Act 2020 provides that a council must develop, adopt and keep in force our governance rules. And those governance rules contain a range of matters, including importantly, the conduct of council meetings. Except as provided in the act and subject to those governance rules, the conduct of council meetings is at the discretion of council. It's not uncommon for councils and other levels of government to commence their proceedings with a prayer. While that practice does vary at present, the courts have made no determination on whether the commencement of proceedings with a prayer is illegal. It's also important to note that the practice does not invalidate the business conducted during the council meeting. In relation to question two, the council prayer is deliberately non-denominational and therefore designed to include all religious faiths as opposed to excluding parts of our community. It is of course up to the individual to reflect on what this means for them. In addition to our prayer, Manningham Council also includes an acknowledgement of country and a statement of diverse backgrounds and cultures which acknowledge all sectors of the community at the commencement of our meeting.
